summary: This document defines a new Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Data Item for traffic classification. It identifies flows from frame or packet content, such as a destination address, and is designed to be extensible and reusable.

eli5.summary: Mail sorters read an address to decide which bin a letter goes into. This lets a radio and a router agree on how to sort traffic.

questions: how does dlep classify flows by dscp
what is a dlep sub-data item
subtitle: A DLEP building block that lets a modem tell a router how to sort traffic into flows by DSCP or Ethernet priority.

tldr.problem: DLEP identifies traffic only by destination endpoint, so a router and modem cannot agree on finer-grained flows that should get different treatment.
tldr.mechanism: A new Traffic Classification Data Item (type 29) carries a traffic classification identifier and a list of Sub-Data Items. Two Sub-Data Items are defined, one listing Diffserv code points and one listing Ethernet VLAN and priority code points.
tldr.outcome: Other DLEP extensions, such as credit window flow control, can reuse this structure instead of defining their own flow identification. Ethernet matches win over Diffserv matches.

today: RFC 9892 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2026, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be used by extensions such as RFC 9893.

sections.title: Why DLEP Needs Traffic Classification
sections.content:
The Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP, RFC 8175) carries link-related control information between two peers, a modem and a router. It defines reusable Data Items, but its flows are identified only by DLEP endpoint. This RFC adds finer-grained flow identification, so a router can use classification information supplied by the modem to recognize flows by data plane header content.

The mechanism is built to pair with uses such as credit window flow control (RFC 9893), and to be shared across several destinations or flows, or used for just one. It is also meant to be reusable by extensions unrelated to credit windows, such as RFC 8651, and to extend later to things like 5-tuple IP flows.

The RFC defines one general Data Item and two Sub-Data Items, one for Differentiated Services Code Points (DSCPs) and one for IEEE 802.1Q Priority Code Points (PCPs).
sections.eli5: Until now the radio and the router could only tell traffic apart by who it was going to. This adds a way to also sort by how urgent it is.

sections.title: TIDs, FIDs and Flows
sections.content:
A Traffic Classification Data Item represents a list of flows that may be used at the same time to give different service classes to traffic sent from a router to a modem. The data plane information for each flow lives in its own Sub-Data Item. The structures are intended to be independent of how the flow identification is used, for example flow control.

Each list of flows has a Traffic Classification Identifier (TID). Each flow has a Flow Identifier (FID). A DLEP destination address is also needed, but it comes from the extension that uses the classification. For example, a modem can supply it in a Destination Up Message using the Credit Window Association Data Item from RFC 9893. TID and FID values have modem-local scope.
sections.eli5: Each set of sorting rules gets a number, and each bin inside it gets its own number too. Only the radio that made the numbers needs them to mean anything.

sections.title: The Traffic Classification Data Item
sections.content:
The modem uses this Data Item to give the router its classification information. When an extension requires it, the modem SHOULD include it in the Session Initialization Response Message, and MAY send updates or new classifications in Session Update Messages. More than one Data Item MAY appear in a message.

The Data Item Type is 29. After the type and length come a 16-bit TID (any value is allowed, with no need for ordering), an 8-bit Num SDIs giving the number of Sub-Data Items, and an 8-bit Reserved field that MUST be zero and is ignored on reception. A Num SDIs of zero is allowed and means no traffic should match this TID. The Length is limited by the supported PDU size.

A router that receives the Data Item looks up the information for that TID. If none exists, it creates a new set from the values received. If some exists, it MUST replace it. In both cases it MUST also update any data plane state tied to the TID.

Each Sub-Data Item shares a common format patterned after the DLEP Data Item: a 16-bit Sub-Data Item Type, a 16-bit Length, then a Value. Their order has no meaning, and parsing errors are handled like any other DLEP Data Item error.
sections.eli5: The radio sends a numbered rule sheet to the router. If the router already has a sheet with that number, it throws the old one away and uses the new one.

sections.title: Diffserv Sub-Data Item
sections.content:
Sub-Data Item Type 1 identifies a set of DSCPs to treat as one flow, so they get the same treatment. It holds a 16-bit FID (the value 0xFFFF is reserved), an 8-bit Num DSCPs, and that many 8-bit DS Fields. Each DS Field carries the DSCP followed by two bits that must be zero. The Length is 3 octets plus the number of DSCPs, so at most 67, and a long list can be split over several Sub-Data Items.

A Num DSCPs of zero is a wildcard that matches any DSCP with no explicit FID. A typical use maps all unlisted DSCPs to a default queue. An implementation that does not support DSCPs and wants the same treatment for everything to a destination indicates zero DSCPs.

On receipt a router MUST validate the information, and a validation failure is an error. It MUST also check that each DS Field value appears only once across the whole Data Item, not just within one Sub-Data Item. A duplicate makes the Data Item an error.
sections.eli5: This rule says that letters stamped with certain urgency marks all go into the same bin, and anything with an unlisted mark goes into the default bin.

sections.title: Ethernet Sub-Data Item
sections.content:
Sub-Data Item Type 2 identifies a VLAN and a set of PCPs to treat as one flow. The IEEE 802.1Q tag has a 3-bit PCP and a 12-bit VLAN Identifier (VID). The item holds a 16-bit FID (again 0xFFFF is reserved), a 4-bit NumPCPs, a 12-bit VID, and a list of 4-bit Priority Fields, each a PCP followed by a bit that must be zero. If NumPCPs is odd, a 4-bit Pad set to zero is added. The maximum number of PCPs is 8, which makes the Length at most 8 octets.

As with Diffserv, zero PCPs is a wildcard for any PCP without an explicit FID. A VID of 0x000 means ignore the VID, and 0xFFF is reserved. Other values from 0x001 through 0xFFE can be used. Explicitly mapped VLANs match first, and the rest fall to this default mapping.

The router MUST validate the item, including any usage-specific rules such as those in RFC 9893, and MUST check that each Priority Field value appears only once across the whole Data Item. When a packet matches both a Diffserv item and an Ethernet item, the TID of the matching VLAN/PCP MUST be used.
sections.eli5: This is the same idea for network switches: sort by a lane number and a priority mark. If both kinds of rule match, the switch rule wins.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
The new formats are used only when an extension requires them. Unexpected appearances of the Data Items are handled as RFC 8175 already defines.

The finer-grained flow identification exposes vulnerabilities similar to existing DLEP messages. For example, an attacker posing as a DLEP peer could inject a different Traffic Classification Data Item and change how traffic maps to queues, causing delay, congestion or loss in some service classes. The transport-layer mechanisms in RFC 8175, the latest BCP 195, IEEE 802.1AE and IEEE 802.1X can be applied, and Layer 2 security can also be used with some updates.
sections.eli5: If a stranger could pretend to be the radio and hand over fake sorting rules, urgent mail could end up in the wrong bin. The usual locks and ID checks used for DLEP help prevent that.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned Data Item Type 29, named Traffic Classification, from the Specification Required range in the DLEP Data Item Type Values registry. IANA also created a new registry, Traffic Classification Sub-Data Item Type Values. Types 1 to 65407 use Specification Required and 65408 to 65534 are Private Use. Initially 1 is Diffserv, 2 is Ethernet, 0 and 65535 are Reserved, and 3 to 65407 are unassigned.

New entries need documentation and approval by a designated expert, who checks that the use is unambiguous, does not conflict with other IETF work and has been reviewed by the MANET Working Group. Requests for new entries are not expected to be frequent. The RFC also recommends that its registration guidance apply to every Specification Required registry in the DLEP Parameters group.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of rule types. Two are filled in, and a few experts decide if anyone wants to add more.

fields.desc: Must be zero; ignored on receipt.
